references_named: Robert Rauschenberg, Erased de Kooning Drawing (1953)
Walter Benjamin, The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction (1935)
rationale: The mechanism is genuinely the argument: the user-agent stylesheet's default rendering of <del>/<ins> is the pentimento, and the clipboard carrying the struck-through text is the X-ray. Concept and execution collapse cleanly (P1), the build is minimal (P3), and the inversion of Rauschenberg's erasure is a precise narrative move that answers a specific prior work. Double-coding works at both depths (P7). The piece is restrained, dry, and intelligent in tone. G6 holds: it is materially distinct from Erased (No Undo) — that work withholds undo and persists erasure to localStorage; this one refuses erasure entirely and smuggles the correction through the clipboard.
reservations: Novelty is moderate rather than high: the <del>/<ins> default rendering is a well-known web-native behavior, and the 'clipboard carries what the eye doesn't' move echoes several existing source-vs-render works in the catalogue (Silencio, Non-finito, Schreibzeit, Incipit). The piece is closer to a clean, well-executed riff on that family than a fully new ontology. The self-deflating artist's statement is witty but slightly thin as a surface — the joke is small and the depth is real, which is correct, but the surface could carry more.
revision_suggestion: To strengthen novelty, consider adding a second web-native mechanism that is genuinely new to the catalogue — e.g., a per-visit <del> count that is itself a <del>/<ins> pair (the ledger self-correcting on reload), or a CSS :visited-style history of past corrections that the browser alone can read. Even a small additional axis would lift this from a strong riff to a standalone node.
